summary:
The Field Shift web application provides farmers and agronomists with information on planting, irrigation and other management decisions based on historical rainfall for their fields (NASA POWER), surface soil moisture, root-zone water content for the next five days, Sentinel-2 satellite images and the corresponding NDVI. The application also compares up to six crop-rotation plans based on water deficit, irrigation requirement and soil cover.

Behind the interface are a FAO-56 layered water balance model for the water forecast and rotation comparison, an AquaCrop-based scenario planner and a field-boundary detection model. Research models tested on NOAA and USDA soil probes include a soil moisture correction using NASA SMAP L3 retrievals and a “water before flowering” outlook based on 34 years of NASA POWER weather data.

All values are explained by the field-aware assistant with information on the source, date, resolution and whether the information was validated for the user’s region or not. Values from model estimates are not shown outside of the region where they were validated, especially for water stress around flowering, one of the biggest causes of yield loss. Farmers need to verify information about their crops rather than rely on a “black box”.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Field Shift is a field planning application for farmers and agronomists. It allows users to compare dated crop plans, identify potential water constraints and see the evidence behind every estimate. All features are accessible in a single workspace.
• Fields — draw or edit field boundaries, request a field-boundary detection model to suggest boundaries, record planted areas, view dated Sentinel-2 imagery and vegetation indices, inspect surface soil moisture, and explore potential downhill flow directions from Copernicus DEM.
• Analytics — inspect historical and five-day root-zone water balances, cumulative water budgets, field priorities, rainfall history compared with a ten-year NASA POWER baseline, and the outlook for water before flowering.
• Strategies — compare two or three dated crop-rotation plans using 13 crop profiles, examining modeled water deficits, irrigation schedules, stress days and soil-cover days. Planting calendars and a crop-area allocation tool support planning across fields.
• Agent — ask questions in the context of a field. Structured evidence supplies sources, dates, units, spatial resolution and validation status for every value.
• Farm — manage shared settings, team roles and access.

HOW IT WORKS
The Field Shift application is a React TypeScript project built on top of Vite and Leaflet. The application is powered by a Python FastAPI backend, a PostgreSQL database and a number of background workers running in Redis/Celery. All of these components are deployed using Docker Compose.
The crop-rotation comparisons use a layered water-balance engine. Scenario planning uses an AquaCrop-based service, and PCSE/WOFOST serves as an offline reference model for checking it. The application also uses a field-boundary detection model to propose outlines that the user can review and save.
NASA POWER is used to provide the rainfall history for the field of interest, as well as climatic context for the location. Two research models developed by the team are used in the application.

1. Surface soil moisture, 0–5 cm.
The application uses LightGBM to correct the ERA5-Land anomalies with NASA SMAP L3 Enhanced retrievals that have been quality-screened. The data used for the model has been restricted to that which would be available operationally, i.e. with a two-day minimum observation age. Quantile models with conformal calibration provide an 80% prediction interval.
The surface soil moisture model was successfully released after having passed the spatial and temporal holdout tests as well as the cross-network checks. The RMSE decreased from 0.101 to 0.098 m³/m³ at 35 new stations in 2025 and from 0.074 to 0.071 m³/m³ on nine independent Iowa farms with 87–99% interval coverage. The leakage test showed that the improvement is indeed due to the real temporal signal in the SMAP observations and that shuffling them in time removes the improvement. With a soil probe on the field, a rolling level offset reduces the error further, to 0.041 m³/m³ at the new stations.

2. Water before flowering.
A layered water balance on USDA SSURGO soil profiles is run with an ensemble of 34 historical NASA POWER weather years, and a phenology step estimates the flowering date. Flowering dates were calibrated against USDA NASS Iowa crop progress for 1991–2010 and tested on 2011–2025, with mean absolute errors of 1.8 days for maize and 3.9 days for soybean.
The outlook for water before flowering provides the probability that the soil water storage in the top metre of soil for the period 10–31 July will fall into the driest third of years for a given location. Hindcasts at 47 USCRN/SCAN stations, evaluated as new locations, show that the outlook outperforms climatology with Brier skill scores of 0.10 from 15 June and 0.20 from 1 July. The skill increases to 0.40 when an in-field soil observation is available.
Both models return their results in the assistant's data contract, so every value carries its source, model version and validation.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Field Shift helps users compare plans before committing seed, water and machinery, identify water constraints ahead of the most sensitive crop stage, and decide what to inspect or measure next. Evidence and uncertainty are visible, so decisions rest on information farmers can check.

CREATIVITY
The project connects crop planning, NASA Earth-observation data and a field-aware assistant in one workspace. Its distinctive feature is the link between each estimate and its provenance: users can see where a value came from, when it applies and how it was evaluated.
Our research combines NASA satellite soil moisture, reanalysis, 34 years of NASA POWER weather and crop phenology, and every model is measured against simple baselines under predefined release rules.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
We considered data latency, spatial resolution, missing satellite observations, leakage in validation, transfer between monitoring networks and differences between regional estimates and field measurements. Additionally, we considered data-source licensing, server-side credentials, field-access controls and usability on desktop and mobile devices.

SCOPE
The accuracy of the models has been validated in the US Midwest. In other regions, the source data are shown without model estimates. Crop-plan comparisons are decision scenarios rather than yield or profit forecasts.
